## Introduction

The goal of this project is to understand how temperature heterogeneity within the city influences phenological events, such as the start of season (SOS) and end of season (EOS), for various tree genera and species in urban environments. To achieve this, I apply spatial statistical models as described below:

$$y(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}} \boldsymbol{\beta} + w(\mathbf{s}_i) + u(\mathbf{t}) + \epsilon(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$$

where $y(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$ represents the phenological event (e.g., SOS or EOS) at location $\mathbf{s}_i$ and time $\mathbf{t}$.$\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}} = [1, \text{AvgTemp}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}, \text{Precp}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}, \text{srad}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}]$ is the vector of predictors. $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3)^\top$ are the regression coefficients for the intercept and covariates. $\beta_1$ is the coefficient for the average temperature (winter for SOS and summer for EOS, respectively), which is the main interest in this study. The spatial random effect $w(\mathbf{s}_i)$ accounts for spatial autocorrelation among locations, while the temporal random effect $u(\mathbf{t})$ captures random year effect. Finally, $\epsilon(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$ represents the residual error term.

This document adopts the same workflow for analyzing urban phenology data, with the key modification of **climate data source**. The aim is to provide a basis for discussion regarding the advantages and limitations of using different datasets (WU, Daymet and HUMID) in urban phenology studies. New York City is selected as the case-study area for comparison. Phenological observations of individual trees derived from remote sensing are available for 2017–2024.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| include: false
#| warning: false

# Install and load 'zhulabtools' package
library(zhulabtools)

# Manage packages: check, install, and load specific packages
check_install_packages(c("dplyr","lubridate", "ggplot2", "sf","sp", "readr", "purrr", "stringr","glue", "tidyr", "broom","lme4", "broom.mixed", "ppcor", "spdep", "spatialreg", "lmtest","car", "spBayes", "coda", "patchwork", "performance", "terra", "ggpmisc", "gstat", "ggmcmc", "taxize", "stats", "viridis"))
if (!require(plotbiomes)) {
  devtools::install_github("valentinitnelav/plotbiomes")
}
load_packages(c("rgbif", "dplyr","lubridate", "ggplot2", "sf","sp", "readr", "purrr", "stringr","glue", "tidyr", "broom","lme4", "broom.mixed", "ppcor", "spdep", "spatialreg", "lmtest","car", "spBayes", "coda", "patchwork", "performance", "terra", "ggpmisc", "gstat", "ggmcmc", "taxize", "stats", "viridis","INLA"))

select <- dplyr::select # Avoid masking by base R's select function
city <- "NY" # Set the city for analysis
phe_types <- c("SOS", "EOS")

source("~/phenology-urban/script/spatial_stats_model/inla_alg/run_sp_inla.R")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: false
valid_HUMID_Daymet <- readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/HUMID/temp_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
  rename(temp_humid = value) |>
  left_join(readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/HUMID/prcp_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
              rename(prcp_humid = value),
            by = c("id", "date")) |>
  left_join(readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/HUMID/srad_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
              rename(srad_humid = value),
            by = c("id", "date")) |>
  left_join(readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/Daymet/monthly2016-2024/tmax_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
              select(id, value, date) |>
              rename(tmax_daymet = value), 
            by = c("id", "date")) |>
  left_join(readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/Daymet/monthly2016-2024/tmin_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
              select(id, value, date) |>
              rename(tmin_daymet = value),
            by = c("id", "date")) |>
  left_join(readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/Daymet/monthly2016-2024/prcp_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
              select(id, value, date) |>
              rename(prcp_daymet = value), 
            by = c("id", "date")) |>
  left_join(readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/NY/Daymet/monthly2016-2024/srad_monthly_all_tree.rds") |>
              select(id, value, date) |>
              rename(srad_daymet = value),
            by = c("id", "date")) |>
  mutate(temp_daymet = (tmax_daymet + tmin_daymet) / 2,
         temp_humid = as.numeric(temp_humid),
         prcp_humid = as.numeric(prcp_humid),
         srad_humid = as.numeric(srad_humid)) |>
  select(id, date, temp_humid, temp_daymet, prcp_humid, prcp_daymet, srad_humid, srad_daymet) |>
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("03", "04", "05") ~ "spring",
      substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("06", "07", "08") ~ "summer",
      substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("09", "10", "11") ~ "fall",
      substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("12", "01", "02") ~ "winter"
    )) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(substr(date, 1, 4)),
         year = if_else(substr(date, 6, 7) == "12", year + 1, year)) |>
  group_by(id, year, season) |>
  summarise(
  # Use sum for prcp, and mean for tmax and tmin
  temp_humid_avg = mean(temp_humid, na.rm = TRUE),
  temp_daymet_avg = mean(temp_daymet, na.rm = TRUE),
  prcp_humid_sum = sum(prcp_humid, na.rm = TRUE),
  prcp_daymet_sum = sum(prcp_daymet, na.rm = TRUE),
  srad_humid_avg = mean(srad_humid, na.rm = TRUE),
  srad_daymet_avg = mean(srad_daymet, na.rm = TRUE),
  .groups = "drop"
) |>
  filter(year > 2016 & year < 2019)

saveRDS(valid_HUMID_Daymet, "~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/NY/valid_HUMID_Daymet.rds")
```

## Data source comparison

Weather Underground (WU) data were obtained from the [Weather Underground program](https://www.wunderground.com/), drawing on multiple personal weather stations located within New York City. These data include daily measurements of temperature and precipitation. For the analysis using WU, **trees located within a 500 m buffer around the WU stations** were selected.

Daymet data were accessed via the [Daymet](https://daymet.ornl.gov/), which provides gridded daily weather data at a spatial resolution of 1 km². For this comparison, I extracted daily maximum and minimum temperature as well as precipitation data for the same period (2016–2023).

HUMID data were accessed from @humid_data, which provides urban-corrected daily weather data at a spatial resolution of 1 km². For this comparison, I extracted the daily maximum and minimum temperature 2 m estimated air temperature after bias correction as well as precipitation rate (kg m⁻² s⁻¹) and daily mean downward shortwave forcing at the surface (W m⁻²) for the overlapping period (2017–2018).

### WU and Daymet temperature comparison

The figure below illustrates the direct comparison between the two datasets, focusing on the average seasonal temperature for trees within the WU buffer. The left panel shows the average winter temperature for the start of season (SOS) and the right panel displays the average summer temperature for the end of season (EOS). The x-axis represents the temperature from the WU data, while the y-axis represents the corresponding Daymet data. The red line represents a 1:1 relationship, indicating where the two datasets align perfectly ([@fig-compare-we-daymet]). Each point represents a tree-year observation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-we-daymet
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-cap: "The comparison of temperature data from Weather Underground (WU) and Daymet for trees within the WU buffer in New York City"
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

source("~/phenology-urban/script/spatial_stats_model/tidy_data.R")
# compare 2 temp/prcp
valid_WU_Daymet <- readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/NY/valid_WU_Daymet.rds")
wu_daymet_winter <- ggplot(data = valid_climate(valid_WU_Daymet, "SOS")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = temp_winter, y = temp_d_winter), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Weather Underground", y = "Daymet") +
  ggtitle("Winter temperature for SOS") +
  theme_minimal()
wu_daymet_summer <- ggplot(data = valid_climate(valid_WU_Daymet, "EOS")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = temp_summer, y = temp_d_summer), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Weather Underground", y = "Daymet") +
  ggtitle("Summer temperature for EOS") +
  theme_minimal()

wu_daymet_winter + wu_daymet_summer
```

Overall, the Daymet data show good alignment with the WU data. However, Daymet tends to report slightly lower temperatures than WU in both winter and summer (as indicated by most points falling below the 1:1 reference line). In winter, WU data exhibit a greater number of outliers, which may reflect the variability and less standardized measurement protocols of personal weather stations.

### WU and HUMID temperature comparison

For those samples both have HUMID and the WU data, the HUMID temperature show good alignment with the WU temperature, especially in winter. However, HUMID tends to report slightly higher temperatures than WU in summer (as indicated by most points falling above the 1:1 reference line) ([@fig-compare-wu-humid]). WU data exhibit a greater number of outliers, which may reflect the variability and less standardized measurement protocols of personal weather stations. Each point represents a tree-year observation. Since the HUMID data only cover 2017-2018, the sample size is smaller than the previous comparison.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-wu-humid
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-cap: "The comparison of temperature data from Weather Underground (WU) and HUMID for trees within the WU buffer in New York City"
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

valid_WU_HUMID <- readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/NY/valid_HUMID_Daymet.rds") |>
  filter(season %in% c("winter", "summer")) |>
  select(id, year, season, temp_humid_avg) |>
  na.omit() |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = season,
    values_from = temp_humid_avg,
    names_prefix = "temp_humid_"
  ) |> 
  right_join(valid_WU_Daymet,
             by = c("id", "year"))

wu_humid_winter <- ggplot(data = valid_climate(valid_WU_HUMID, "SOS")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = temp_winter, y = temp_humid_winter), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Weather Underground", y = "HUMID") +
  ggtitle("Winter temperature for SOS") +
  theme_minimal()
wu_humid_summer <- ggplot(data = valid_climate(valid_WU_HUMID, "EOS")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = temp_summer, y = temp_humid_summer), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Weather Underground", y = "HUMID") +
  ggtitle("Summer temperature for EOS") +
  theme_minimal()

wu_humid_winter + wu_humid_summer
```

### HUMID and Daymet comparison

In this section, I compare the temperature, precipitation, and shortwave radiation from HUMID and Daymet for all available trees in New York City. Each point represents a tree-year observation.

**Temperature**

Daymet reports lower temperatures than HUMID in both winter and summer (as indicated by most points falling beyond the 1:1 reference line). In summer, the variation of HUMID temperature is larger than that of Daymet, which may reflect the influence of urban heat islands and localized temperature variations captured by HUMID ([@fig-compare-humid-daymet1]).

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-humid-daymet1
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-cap: "The comparison of temperature data from HUMID and Daymet for all available trees in New York City"
#| warning: false
#| eval: true


valid_HUMID_Daymet <- readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/NY/valid_HUMID_Daymet.rds") |>
  filter(season %in% c("winter", "summer")) |>
  mutate(year = as.factor(year)) |>
  na.omit()

split_by_type <- valid_HUMID_Daymet %>%
  group_by(season) %>%
  group_split()

# Define a function to fit and plot each case
plot_weighted_fit <- function(df) {
  type_name <- unique(df$season)
  model <- lm(temp_humid_avg ~ temp_daymet_avg, data = df)
  df$fitted <- predict(model)

  slope <- round(coef(model)[2], 3)
  intercept <- round(coef(model)[1], 3)
  R_squared <- round(summary(model)$r.squared, 3)

  annot_label <- paste0("y = ", slope, "x + ",intercept, "\nR^2 = ", R_squared)

  ggplot(df, aes(x = temp_daymet_avg, y = temp_humid_avg)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = year), alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text",
             x = min(df$temp_daymet_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
             y = max(df$temp_humid_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
             label = annot_label,
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 4) +
    labs(
      title = paste(type_name, "temperature"),
      x = "Daymet",
      y = "HUMID"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plots <- lapply(split_by_type, plot_weighted_fit)

plots[[2]] + plots[[1]] +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & 
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

**Precipitation**

The HUMID precipitation data are derived from a combination of daily gridded precipitation analysis data, PRISM long-term climatologies, and temporal disaggregation using radar, satellite, or reanalysis data based on availability, whereas Daymet precipitation data are based directly on selected weather stations with additional quality control constraints. So I believe Daymet provides more reliable precipitation estimates for the analysis.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-humid-daymet3
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-cap: "The comparison of precipitation data from HUMID and Daymet for all available trees in New York City"
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

# Define a function to fit and plot each case
plot_weighted_fit <- function(df) {
  type_name <- unique(df$season)
  model <- lm(prcp_humid_sum ~ prcp_daymet_sum, data = df)
  df$fitted <- predict(model)

  slope <- round(coef(model)[2], 3)
  intercept <- round(coef(model)[1], 3)
  R_squared <- round(summary(model)$r.squared, 3)

  annot_label <- paste0("y = ", slope, "x + ",intercept, "\nR^2 = ", R_squared)

  ggplot(df, aes(x = prcp_daymet_sum, y = prcp_humid_sum)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = year), alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text",
             x = min(df$prcp_daymet_sum, na.rm = TRUE),
             y = max(df$prcp_humid_sum, na.rm = TRUE),
             label = annot_label,
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 4) +
    labs(
      title = paste(type_name, "precipitation"),
      x = "Daymet (mm)",
      y = "HUMID (kg/m² s)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plots <- lapply(split_by_type, plot_weighted_fit)

plots[[2]] + plots[[1]] +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & 
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

**Shortwave radiation**

Unlike Daymet, which estimates shortwave radiation indirectly using an empirical relationship with the Tmax and Tmin, HUMID uses downscaled radiation inputs from the NLDAS-2 reanalysis, which includes the effects of cloud cover and atmospheric conditions. This physically driven modeling framework makes HUMID better suited for capturing the spatial variability and complexity of urban energy balance.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-humid-daymet2
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-cap: "The comparison of shortwave data from HUMID and Daymet for all available trees in New York City"
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

# Define a function to fit and plot each case
plot_weighted_fit <- function(df) {
  type_name <- unique(df$season)
  model <- lm(srad_humid_avg ~ srad_daymet_avg, data = df)
  df$fitted <- predict(model)

  slope <- round(coef(model)[2], 3)
  intercept <- round(coef(model)[1], 3)
  R_squared <- round(summary(model)$r.squared, 3)

  annot_label <- paste0("y = ", slope, "x + ",intercept, "\nR^2 = ", R_squared)

  ggplot(df, aes(x = srad_daymet_avg, y = srad_humid_avg)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = year), alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text",
             x = min(df$srad_daymet_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
             y = max(df$srad_humid_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
             label = annot_label,
             hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 4) +
    labs(
      title = paste(type_name, "shortwave radiation"),
      x = "Daymet",
      y = "HUMID"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plots <- lapply(split_by_type, plot_weighted_fit)

plots[[2]] + plots[[1]] +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & 
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

<!-- Overall, the spatial statistical models using different data sources and sample sets show consistent patterns in the coefficients of the temperature variable. The temperature coefficients associated with SOS are generally positive, while those associated with EOS are generally negative. This indicates that higher temperatures are linked to an earlier start of season and a later end of season. -->

<!-- However, differences emerge in the magnitude and significance levels of the coefficients. In general, models using HUMID + Daymet data tend to produce coefficients with slightly larger magnitudes compared to those based on WU data for trees within the WU buffer. This may suggest that the WU data capture greater variability in temperature—potentially influenced by outliers in the personal weather station measurements. -->

<!-- It is also important to note that the two datasets are based on different sample sizes. The WU dataset includes only the points within the defined buffer, whereas the HUMID dataset currently provides data extending through 2018. -->

## Discussion

This document records the differences between climate datasets. To further evaluate the suitability of each dataset and inform future data selection, I summarize the key characteristics of both datasets as follows:

-   **HUMID** data: HUMID tends to report higher temperatures and a wider range of variation compared to Daymet data, with fewer extreme outliers compared to WU data. It seems to capture the urban heat island and temperature heterogeneity well, as it conduct the urban bias correction. It has finer spatial resolution (1 km²) and uniform spatial coverage across the study area. However, the data only extends to 2018, meaning that only the years 2017–2018 overlap with the remote sensing observations.

-   **Daymet** data: Daymet tends to report slightly lower temperatures and a narrower range of variation compared to WU data, with fewer extreme outliers. It has finer spatial resolution (1 km²) and uniform spatial coverage across the study area.

-   **Weather Underground (WU)** data: WU data generally report slightly higher temperatures and a broader range of variation than Daymet, with more extreme outliers, likely due to less standardized measurement practices of personal weather stations. The data may be limited by the number of available stations, especially in smaller cities, and their uneven spatial distribution. Further analyses require defining a buffer around stations to select relevant trees.

I still have some remaining questions regarding the datasets:

-   How well do these datasets capture precipitation and shortwave? Given coverage and resolution, can Daymet resolve their within-city heterogeneity?

-   If interpolate Weather Underground PWS data to a surface, could that compete with spatial random effects in my further phenology models?
